_link.title: I can explain the role of stomata and guard cells in regulating transpiration

options.text: A pore in the leaf surface bordered by two guard cells
A specialised root cell that absorbs water
A layer of waxy coating on the leaf surface
A vessel element found in xylem tissue

explanations.a: Correct. A stoma is a pore in the leaf epidermis bordered by two guard cells that control its opening and closing.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A specialised root cell that absorbs water is a root hair cell, not a stoma.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A waxy coating on the leaf surface is the cuticle, not a stoma.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Vessel elements are found in xylem tissue. A stoma is a pore in the leaf surface.

toLevel2.stem: What happens to a stoma when guard cells become turgid?

options.text: The stoma opens
The stoma closes
The stoma is destroyed
The stoma moves to the upper epidermis

explanations.a: Correct. When water enters guard cells and they become turgid, the stoma opens, allowing gas exchange.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Turgid guard cells cause the stoma to open, not close. The stoma closes when guard cells are flaccid.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Guard cells becoming turgid is a normal process that opens the stoma; it does not destroy it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stomata do not move location. Turgidity of guard cells causes the stoma to open.

toLevel2.stem: What causes guard cells to become flaccid and close the stoma?

options.text: Water leaving the guard cells by osmosis
Water entering the guard cells by osmosis
Sugar being produced by photosynthesis
Minerals being absorbed by the roots

explanations.a: Correct. When water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water entering guard cells makes them turgid, which opens the stoma rather than closing it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sugar production by photosynthesis does not directly cause guard cells to become flaccid.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Mineral absorption by roots is unrelated to the opening and closing of guard cells.

toLevel2.stem: What is the biggest factor affecting the rate of transpiration?

options.text: The number of open stomata in the leaves
The length of the plant's roots
The thickness of the xylem walls
The amount of sugar in the phloem

explanations.a: Correct. By far the biggest factor affecting the rate of transpiration is the number of open stomata present in the leaves.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Root length affects water uptake but is not the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Xylem wall thickness relates to structural support, not the rate of transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Sugar content in the phloem is part of translocation, not transpiration.

toLevel2.stem: Which two gases are exchanged through open stomata?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Methane and oxygen
Helium and carbon dioxide

explanations.a: Correct. Open stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis and oxygen to exit as a by-product.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Nitrogen and hydrogen are not the primary gases exchanged through stomata in plant leaves.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Methane is not a gas typically exchanged through stomata during photosynthesis or respiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Helium is an inert gas and is not involved in plant gas exchange through stomata.

toLevel2.stem: Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Correct. A stoma is composed of two guard cells that control its opening and closing through changes in turgor pressure.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Guard cells do control stomata. When guard cells gain water they become turgid and the stoma opens; when they lose water they become flaccid and it closes.

toLevel2.stem: When guard cells are flaccid, the stoma is open and gas exchange occurs.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Incorrect. When guard cells are flaccid, they cover the stoma and no exchange can take place. The stoma opens when guard cells are turgid.
explanations.b: Correct. When guard cells are flaccid, the stoma is closed and gas exchange cannot occur. The stoma opens only when guard cells are turgid.

toLevel2.stem: A stoma is composed of two {{blank:1}} that control its opening and closing.
When water enters guard cells, they become {{blank:1}} and the stoma opens.
Opening stomata allows {{blank:1}} to enter the leaf for photosynthesis.

toLevel3.stem: Why do guard cells close stomata on a hot, dry day?

options.text: To reduce water loss by transpiration when the risk of dehydration is high
To increase the rate of photosynthesis during peak sunlight
To allow more carbon dioxide into the leaf for energy
To trap heat inside the leaf for faster chemical reactions

explanations.a: Correct. On a hot, dry day, guard cells lose water to surrounding cells by osmosis, becoming flaccid and closing stomata to reduce water loss through transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Closing stomata actually limits photosynthesis because it restricts CO₂ entry into the leaf.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Closing stomata prevents carbon dioxide entry, reducing photosynthesis rather than increasing it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stomatal closure is about conserving water, not trapping heat inside the leaf.

toLevel3.stem: What trade-off do plants face when they close their stomata?

options.text: They conserve water but limit carbon dioxide entry for photosynthesis
They increase transpiration but reduce mineral absorption
They absorb more water but lose minerals through the leaves
They speed up photosynthesis but slow down respiration

explanations.a: Correct. Closing stomata prevents water loss through transpiration but also limits CO₂ uptake, which slows photosynthesis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Closing stomata reduces transpiration rather than increasing it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomatal closure does not increase water absorption or cause mineral loss through leaves.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Closing stomata slows photosynthesis because less CO₂ enters the leaf.

toLevel3.stem: How does the process of osmosis relate to guard cell function?

options.text: Water moves into or out of guard cells by osmosis, changing their turgor and opening or closing the stoma
Osmosis forces carbon dioxide into guard cells to trigger stomatal opening
Osmosis breaks down guard cell walls, permanently opening the stoma
Osmosis moves sugars into guard cells to provide energy for stomatal movement

explanations.a: Correct. Guard cells open and close via osmosis: water entry makes them turgid (stoma opens) and water loss makes them flaccid (stoma closes).
explanations.b: Incorrect. Osmosis involves water movement, not carbon dioxide. CO₂ enters through the open stoma, not through guard cells by osmosis.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Osmosis does not break down cell walls. Guard cell walls remain intact as water moves in and out.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Osmosis involves water movement, not sugar transport. Guard cells change shape due to water content.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the number of open stomata have such a large effect on transpiration rate?

options.text: More open stomata increase the surface area through which water vapour can escape
More open stomata increase the rate of photosynthesis in roots
Open stomata pump water actively out of the leaf
Open stomata absorb sunlight, heating the leaf and increasing evaporation

explanations.a: Correct. The more stomata are open, the greater the surface area available for water vapour loss, directly increasing the transpiration rate.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Stomata affect gas exchange in leaves, not photosynthesis in roots. Roots do not photosynthesise.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomata do not actively pump water. Transpiration is a passive process driven by evaporation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While leaf temperature does affect transpiration, stomata do not absorb sunlight themselves.

toLevel3.stem: What is the role of the cuticle in relation to stomatal regulation of water loss?

options.text: The cuticle is a waxy waterproof coating that reduces water loss from leaf surfaces other than stomata
The cuticle opens and closes stomata in response to light
The cuticle transports water from the xylem to the guard cells
The cuticle absorbs water from the air to keep guard cells turgid

explanations.a: Correct. The cuticle is a waxy, waterproof coating that reduces water loss from the leaf surface, meaning most water loss occurs through stomata.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The cuticle does not control stomata. Guard cells are responsible for opening and closing stomata.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The cuticle is a surface coating and does not transport water. Xylem handles water transport.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The cuticle prevents water loss rather than absorbing water from the environment.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important for a plant to balance the opening and closing of its stomata?

options.text: Because plants need CO₂ for photosynthesis but must also conserve water
Because plants need to release oxygen but must absorb nitrogen
Because open stomata increase root pressure and may damage cells
Because stomata must remain shut at night to allow respiration

explanations.a: Correct. Opening stomata allows CO₂ entry for photosynthesis but also increases water loss. Closing them conserves water but limits CO₂ uptake. Balance is essential.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Plants do release oxygen, but nitrogen absorption is not a function of stomata.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomatal opening does not increase root pressure to damaging levels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Plants carry out respiration continuously, and stomatal behaviour is primarily linked to water conservation and CO₂ uptake.

toLevel3.stem: Closing stomata reduces both transpiration and the rate of photosynthesis.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Correct. Closing stomata prevents water loss through transpiration but also limits CO₂ entry, which slows photosynthesis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Closing stomata does reduce both processes because stomata are the main route for both water vapour exit and CO₂ entry.

toLevel3.stem: On a hot dry day, guard cells lose water by {{blank:1}}, becoming flaccid and closing the stomata.
Closing stomata reduces water loss but also limits the entry of {{blank:1}} needed for photosynthesis.
The more stomata in leaves and the more {{blank:1}} they are, the greater the surface area for water vapour loss.

toLevel4.stem: A student notices that a potted plant wilts on a hot afternoon but recovers by early morning. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.text: Water loss through open stomata exceeds root uptake during the day, but stomata close at night allowing the plant to rehydrate
The plant produces extra sugar during the day which draws water out of cells
Xylem vessels break down in heat and repair overnight
Roots stop absorbing water when the soil is warm

explanations.a: Correct. During the hot day, stomata are open for photosynthesis and transpiration exceeds water uptake, causing wilting. At night stomata close, transpiration slows, and the plant rehydrates.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While sugar production occurs during photosynthesis, it does not directly cause wilting in this way.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Xylem vessels are reinforced with lignin and do not break down and repair on a daily cycle.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Roots continue absorbing water in warm soil. The wilting is caused by transpiration exceeding uptake.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher applies petroleum jelly to the lower surface of leaves on Plant A but not Plant B. Both plants are placed in identical sunny conditions. What result would you predict?

options.text: Plant A loses less water because the jelly blocks stomata on the lower epidermis
Plant A loses more water because the jelly heats the leaf surface
Plant B loses less water because it has no barrier to slow evaporation
Both plants lose the same amount of water because the cuticle controls all water loss

explanations.a: Correct. Petroleum jelly blocks stomata on the lower epidermis, reducing the surface area for water vapour loss and lowering the transpiration rate in Plant A.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Petroleum jelly blocks stomata rather than heating the leaf, so it reduces rather than increases water loss.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Without a barrier, Plant B would have more open stomata and therefore greater transpiration, not less.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Most water loss occurs through stomata, not the cuticle. Blocking stomata significantly reduces transpiration.

toLevel4.stem: A desert plant has very few stomata and a thick cuticle. How do these adaptations help it survive?

options.text: They minimise water loss through transpiration in an environment where water is scarce
They maximise photosynthesis by trapping more carbon dioxide inside the leaf
They increase the rate of mineral uptake from dry soil
They allow the plant to absorb water from humid night air

explanations.a: Correct. Fewer stomata and a thick cuticle both reduce water loss through transpiration, which is essential for survival in dry environments.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Fewer stomata actually limit CO₂ entry and reduce photosynthesis. The trade-off is worthwhile because water conservation is more critical.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomata and cuticle thickness do not directly affect mineral uptake from the soil.
explanations.d: Incorrect. These adaptations prevent water loss rather than increasing water absorption from the air.

toLevel4.stem: A student measures transpiration rate in a leafy shoot and finds it drops sharply at midday despite high light intensity. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Guard cells lost water due to extreme heat, becoming flaccid and closing stomata to conserve water
The xylem ran out of water at midday and could not supply the leaves
Photosynthesis stopped at midday so the stomata were no longer needed
The cuticle melted in the heat, sealing all leaf pores

explanations.a: Correct. At midday, high temperatures cause guard cells to lose water rapidly through osmosis, becoming flaccid and closing stomata. This reduces transpiration despite high light intensity.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The xylem maintains a continuous water column through cohesion-tension; it does not simply run out at midday.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Photosynthesis does not stop at midday. The reduction in transpiration is due to stomatal closure from water stress.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The waxy cuticle does not melt at normal environmental temperatures.

toLevel4.stem: If a plant's guard cells were unable to undergo osmosis, what would be the most likely consequence?

options.text: Stomata would remain in a fixed state and the plant could not regulate transpiration or gas exchange
The plant would photosynthesise faster because stomata would stay permanently open
The plant would absorb more minerals because the stomata would continuously draw water up
The xylem would collapse because there would be no water tension

explanations.a: Correct. Guard cells rely on osmosis to change shape. Without osmosis, they cannot become turgid or flaccid, so the stoma cannot open or close in response to conditions.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Whether stomata would be open or closed depends on the starting state. Either way, the plant could not regulate the balance between photosynthesis and water loss.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Stomatal regulation affects gas exchange and transpiration, not mineral uptake directly.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The xylem structure is maintained by lignin and cohesion of water, not by guard cell osmosis.

toLevel4.stem: Two identical plants are placed in separate environments: one in still, humid air and the other in dry, windy conditions. Which plant would have a higher transpiration rate and why?

options.text: The plant in dry, windy conditions, because wind removes water vapour from around stomata maintaining a steep concentration gradient
The plant in still, humid air, because humidity causes stomata to open wider
Both plants have the same rate because they have equal numbers of stomata
The plant in still, humid air, because water molecules evaporate faster in humid conditions

explanations.a: Correct. In windy conditions, water vapour is removed quickly from around stomata, maintaining a high concentration gradient that drives faster evaporation and transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Humidity does not cause stomata to open wider. High humidity reduces the concentration gradient, slowing transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Even with the same number of stomata, environmental conditions strongly affect transpiration rate.
explanations.d: Incorrect. High humidity means the air already holds more water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient and slowing evaporation.

toLevel4.stem: A gardener moves a fern from a shady spot to full sun. What immediate change in stomatal behaviour would you expect?

options.text: Stomata open wider because light stimulates guard cells to take up water
Stomata close because the plant does not need carbon dioxide in sunlight
Stomata remain unchanged because light does not affect guard cells
Stomata close because intense light damages the guard cell membranes

explanations.a: Correct. Light causes stomata to open wider, allowing greater entry of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. This also increases transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, which is driven by light. Stomata open in light to allow CO₂ entry.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Light is a major factor that causes stomata to open wider for photosynthesis.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Normal sunlight does not damage guard cell membranes. Light stimulates stomatal opening.

toLevel4.stem: A desert plant has fewer stomata and a thicker {{blank:1}} to reduce water loss through transpiration.
In windy conditions, water vapour is removed quickly from around stomata, maintaining a steep {{blank:1}} that drives faster evaporation.
Observations show that the number of open stomata is lowest at {{blank:1}} because guard cells lose water in extreme heat.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that plants would benefit from having no stomata because they would never lose water. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: The claim is flawed because without stomata, no CO₂ could enter for photosynthesis and the plant would be unable to produce glucose
The claim is correct because water conservation is always more important than photosynthesis
The claim is correct because the cuticle can absorb enough CO₂ for photosynthesis
The claim is flawed because stomata only lose water at night when photosynthesis stops

explanations.a: Correct. Without stomata, plants could not take in CO₂ for photosynthesis and would be unable to produce glucose for energy. Stomata are essential despite the water loss trade-off.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While water conservation is important, without photosynthesis the plant cannot produce food and would die.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The cuticle is a waterproof barrier and does not allow significant gas exchange. CO₂ enters primarily through stomata.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Most water loss through stomata occurs during the day when they are open for photosynthesis, not at night.

toLevel5.stem: A scientist observes that a species of cactus opens its stomata at night and closes them during the day. What is the most likely advantage of this strategy?

options.text: It allows CO₂ uptake when temperatures are cooler and humidity is higher, reducing water loss
It increases photosynthesis rate because there is more oxygen available at night
It prevents mineral loss that would occur if stomata were open during the day
It allows the cactus to absorb water vapour from the night air through stomata

explanations.a: Correct. Opening stomata at night when it is cooler and more humid reduces the concentration gradient for water vapour, minimising transpiration while still allowing CO₂ uptake.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Photosynthesis requires light and occurs during the day. These plants store CO₂ taken in at night for daytime photosynthesis.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Minerals are not lost through stomata. This strategy is about conserving water.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stomata are not designed to absorb water vapour. The strategy reduces water loss while still allowing gas exchange.

toLevel5.stem: Two plant species grow in the same habitat. Species X has stomata on both leaf surfaces while Species Y has stomata only on the lower surface. Which analysis best explains this difference?

options.text: Species X likely prioritises maximum gas exchange for rapid growth, while Species Y reduces water loss by limiting stomata to the shaded lower surface
Species X has more xylem tissue than Species Y
Species Y cannot photosynthesise as efficiently because it has fewer stomata
Species X must be a desert plant that needs more stomata to survive

explanations.a: Correct. Stomata on both surfaces maximise CO₂ entry but increase water loss. Stomata only on the lower surface reduce direct sun exposure on stomata, lowering transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Stomatal distribution does not necessarily correlate with the amount of xylem tissue.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While fewer stomata limit CO₂ entry, Species Y may be adapted to conserve water as a higher priority.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Desert plants typically have fewer stomata to conserve water, not more.

toLevel5.stem: A student conducts an experiment and concludes that wind is the most important factor affecting transpiration because their plant lost the most water on a windy day. Evaluate the validity of this conclusion.

options.text: The conclusion is weak because the student did not control other variables like temperature and humidity that also changed on the windy day
The conclusion is valid because wind is the only factor that affects transpiration rate
The conclusion is valid because wind directly opens and closes stomata
The conclusion is weak because wind has no effect on transpiration

explanations.a: Correct. The student's conclusion is weak because multiple factors affect transpiration. A windy day may also be hotter or drier, so the student cannot attribute the result to wind alone without controlling other variables.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Wind is not the only factor. Light intensity, temperature, humidity, and the number of open stomata all affect transpiration rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Wind does not directly open or close stomata. Guard cells control stomata through osmosis. Wind affects the concentration gradient around stomata.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Wind does affect transpiration by removing water vapour from around stomata, but other variables must be controlled to draw valid conclusions.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why observations of stomata over 24 hours show the number of open stomata is lowest at midday, even though light intensity is highest.

options.text: High midday temperatures cause rapid water loss from guard cells, overriding the light stimulus and causing stomatal closure to prevent dehydration
Plants do not need carbon dioxide at midday because they have already stored enough from the morning
The xylem cannot supply water fast enough so it shuts down at midday
Light intensity is actually lowest at midday due to the angle of the sun

explanations.a: Correct. Although light promotes stomatal opening, extreme midday heat causes guard cells to lose water faster than it can be replaced. The resulting flaccidity closes stomata to prevent dangerous water loss.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Plants continuously require CO₂ for photosynthesis during daylight hours. They do not store enough from the morning.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The xylem is a passive transport system that does not shut down. The issue is that water loss exceeds supply at the guard cell level.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Light intensity is typically highest around midday when the sun is at its peak.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that because guard cells contain chloroplasts, they must photosynthesise to generate the energy needed to open stomata. Evaluate this reasoning.

options.text: The reasoning is partially correct that guard cells have chloroplasts and respond to light, but stomatal opening is driven by osmosis rather than by ATP from photosynthesis
The reasoning is entirely correct because guard cells need ATP from photosynthesis to pump water in
The reasoning is entirely wrong because guard cells do not contain chloroplasts
The reasoning is correct because all plant cells photosynthesise to power their functions

explanations.a: Correct. Guard cells do contain chloroplasts and respond to light, but stomatal opening is primarily controlled by water movement through osmosis changing guard cell turgor, not directly by ATP from photosynthesis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While guard cells have chloroplasts, stomatal opening is driven by osmotic water movement changing turgor pressure, not by ATP-powered pumping.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Guard cells do contain chloroplasts, which is one reason they respond to light.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Not all plant cells photosynthesise. Root cells, for example, lack chloroplasts.

toLevel5.stem: A plant is genetically modified so that its guard cells cannot become flaccid. Analyse the likely consequences for the plant in a drought.

options.text: Stomata would remain permanently open, leading to uncontrolled water loss and likely plant death from dehydration
The plant would thrive because it could photosynthesise continuously without interruption
The plant would be unaffected because the cuticle prevents most water loss
The plant would grow faster because roots would absorb more water to compensate

explanations.a: Correct. If guard cells cannot become flaccid, stomata cannot close. During drought, the plant would lose water continuously through transpiration and would likely die from dehydration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While continuous stomatal opening allows CO₂ entry, uncontrolled water loss during drought would kill the plant before any benefit from increased photosynthesis.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Most water loss occurs through stomata, not the cuticle. Permanently open stomata would be fatal during drought.
explanations.d: Incorrect. During drought, soil water is limited. Roots cannot compensate for the massive water loss from permanently open stomata.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate which adaptation would be most effective for a plant living in a hot, arid environment: fewer stomata, stomata only on the lower leaf surface, or a thicker cuticle.

options.text: Fewer stomata, because this directly reduces the surface area for water vapour loss, which is the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate
A thicker cuticle, because most water loss occurs through the cuticle rather than stomata
Stomata only on the lower surface, because the lower surface is always in direct sunlight
All three are equally effective because they all prevent photosynthesis

explanations.a: Correct. Since the number of open stomata is by far the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate, having fewer stomata most directly reduces water loss in an arid environment.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Most water loss occurs through stomata, not the cuticle. A thicker cuticle helps but does not address the main route of water loss.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The lower surface is typically shaded, not in direct sunlight. While this adaptation helps, it does not reduce stomatal number overall.
explanations.d: Incorrect. These adaptations do not equally affect transpiration, and their purpose is to conserve water while still allowing some photosynthesis.

toLevel5.stem: Although light promotes stomatal opening, extreme midday heat overrides this by causing guard cells to lose water, resulting in stomatal {{blank:1}}.
A cactus that opens stomata at night and closes them during the day minimises {{blank:1}} while still allowing CO₂ uptake.
